overview: This two-page file concerns Japanese railway freight-rate policy in 1930. A State Department file note cross-references an August 1 report from Neville in Japan and summarizes proposals intended to counter declining railway revenues while reducing production costs. The attached extract describes two options—a general 20 percent reduction or a sliding reduction of 10 to 20 percent on producing materials—and notes that a separate 20 percent concession had already been extended during the spring to all Japanese export goods, superseding earlier selective reductions for products such as tea.

subfiles.summary: The note directs the reader to file 894.00 P.R./32 for item 219 and identifies an August 1, 1930 communication from Neville in Japan. It says the proposed rate reductions were intended principally to counter declining railway revenues and secondarily to lower production costs. The two alternatives were a general 20 percent reduction and a sliding reduction of 10 to 20 percent on producing materials; a copy is noted as attached.

subfiles.title: Attached extract on Japanese railway freight rates
subfiles.about: An attached extract explains proposed domestic freight-rate reductions and an existing concession for Japanese exports.
subfiles.summary: The extract reports discussion of reducing railway freight rates to address declining revenues while also lowering the public’s cost of production. No definite plan had been adopted, but officials were considering either a 20 percent reduction in all rates or a sliding reduction of 10 to 20 percent on producing materials. These proposals did not concern exports, because a 20 percent railway-rate reduction for all Japanese export goods had already taken effect during the spring, broadening earlier selective concessions such as that for tea.

interest: The file offers a compact view of Japanese railway pricing policy during the economic strains of 1930, showing the apparent paradox of using lower rates to counter declining railway revenues. It is especially useful because it distinguishes proposed domestic reductions from an export subsidy already implemented in the spring and records the transition from commodity-specific concessions, such as reduced rates for tea, to equal treatment of all export goods. The cross-reference sheet also illustrates how substantive diplomatic reporting was excerpted and redistributed within the State Department’s decimal filing system.
